name: The Rood of Grace
summary: Maidstone, Candlemas Eve, 1538: the King's men have exposed Boxley Abbey's weeping mechanical crucifix as a fraud and the crowd has torn it apart. You are the clockmaker who built its works nineteen years ago for a children's play. You walk the High Street through seven stations, getting each part back by bargaining, telling the truth or stealing it, then rebuild the machine at your bench and decide what it is for.
motifs: stations of the cross as a street walk
an inscription hidden inside the pinned drum
thread: Thomas Gale, clockmaker, gathered the pieces of the Rood of Grace (crank, pinned drum, wires, bellows, tin cistern, and maybe its gouged oak face) from the people of Maidstone who had torn it up: a clerk, apprentices, a pedlar, a reforming smith, and Agnes Hollis, a widow who once crawled to it from Rye. Inside the drum he found his own forgotten words: 'It is beech and brass. Do not kneel to it.' Rebuilt, the machine weeps only what someone pours into it. His rage did not go away; it became the weight that drives the clock. Carried: the pinned drum with its inscription, the oak face (or a wet sleeve, if he threw it in the Medway), and perhaps Agnes's empty flask. Still unresolved: who is to blame when a true machine is used to tell a lie, and what an honest thing is worth once everyone has stopped believing in it.
delight: The Rood could only ever weep the water someone put into it. Agnes pouring in holy water she had kept for eleven years and getting back exactly that much, not a drop more, then laughing, is the moment the whole street was walking toward. I also loved that the assembly order ('Heart first. Hand to heart. Tears last, or they rust the heart') works as a puzzle and as a creed at once.

idea.name: The Rood of Grace
idea.premise: In 1538 the Reformation's commissioners exposed Boxley Abbey's moving, weeping crucifix as a clockwork fraud, and a Maidstone crowd tore it to pieces in the street. The clockmaker who built its works in good faith, as a toy for children, walks the High Street station by station to take every part back from the people now holding it with contempt, grief or profit. He rebuilds it once, honestly and with the back left off, and learns it only ever wept what was poured into it.
